cruxes: Whatever begins to exist has a cause
The universe began to exist
NOT: The universe has a cause
arguments.name: Kalam cosmological argument, stage 1
premises: Whatever begins to exist has a cause
arguments.source: W. L. Craig, The Kalam Cosmological Argument (1979); Craig & Sinclair (2009), Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology

cruxes: The cause of the universe is timeless
The cause of the universe is spaceless
Any timeless, spaceless cause of a temporal effect is personal
NOT: The cause is personal
arguments.name: Kalam stage 2: the cause is personal
premises: The cause of the universe is timeless
The cause of the universe is spaceless
Any timeless, spaceless cause of a temporal effect is personal
arguments.source: Craig & Sinclair (2009): a timeless, spaceless cause of a temporal effect must be a personal agent

cruxes: Everything that exists has an explanation of its existence
If the universe has an explanation, that explanation is God
The universe exists
NOT: God exists
arguments.name: Leibnizian contingency argument
premises: Everything that exists has an explanation of its existence
If the universe has an explanation, that explanation is God
arguments.source: G. W. Leibniz, Monadology 32-38 (1714); reconstruction as in Craig, Reasonable Faith (3rd ed. 2008)

cruxes: Necessarily, if a maximally great being exists it exists necessarily (Anselm's principle)
Possibly a maximally great being exists
NOT: A maximally great being exists
arguments.name: Modal ontological argument (Hartshorne, Plantinga)
premises: Necessarily, if a maximally great being exists it exists necessarily (Anselm's principle)
Possibly a maximally great being exists
arguments.source: C. Hartshorne, The Logic of Perfection (1962); A. Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity (1974) ch. X

cruxes: Anselm's principle (as above)
Possibly no maximally great being exists
NOT: No maximally great being exists
arguments.name: Reverse modal ontological argument
premises: Possibly no maximally great being exists
arguments.source: e.g. P. Tidman, Religious Studies 29 (1993); Oppy, Arguing about Gods (2006) ch. 2

cruxes: If God exists, God can prevent all evil
If God exists, God wants to prevent all evil
A being who can and wants to prevent all evil leaves none
Evil exists
NOT: God does not exist
arguments.name: Logical problem of evil (Mackie)
premises: If God exists, God can prevent all evil
If God exists, God wants to prevent all evil
A being who can and wants to prevent all evil leaves none
arguments.source: J. L. Mackie, Evil and Omnipotence, Mind 64 (1955) doi:10.1093/mind/LXIV.254.200

arguments.name: Free will defence: the consistency set
premises: If God exists, God can prevent all evil
If God exists, God wants to prevent evil unless there is a morally sufficient reason
A being who can and wants to prevent all evil leaves none
There is a morally sufficient reason for permitting evil
arguments.source: A. Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil (1974): God wants to prevent evil unless permitting it is needed for a greater good (morally significant freedom)

cruxes: There is suffering an omnipotent, omniscient being could have prevented without losing a greater good
An omniscient, wholly good being would prevent all gratuitous suffering
NOT: God does not exist
arguments.name: Evidential argument from gratuitous suffering (Rowe)
premises: There is suffering an omnipotent, omniscient being could have prevented without losing a greater good
An omniscient, wholly good being would prevent all gratuitous suffering
arguments.source: W. Rowe, The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism, American Philosophical Quarterly 16 (1979) 335-341

conclusion: A perfectly loving God does not exist
cruxes: If a perfectly loving God exists, every non-resisting person can believe God exists
Some non-resisting people do not believe God exists
NOT: A perfectly loving God does not exist
arguments.name: Argument from divine hiddenness
premises: If a perfectly loving God exists, every non-resisting person can believe God exists
Some non-resisting people do not believe God exists
arguments.source: J. L. Schellenberg, Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (Cornell, 1993)

cruxes: A pope teaching ex cathedra cannot teach heresy (Vatican I)
What an ecumenical council condemns as heresy is heretical
Constantinople III condemned Honorius's letter to Sergius as heresy
Honorius's letter was an ex cathedra definition
arguments.name: Pope Honorius and papal infallibility
arguments.note: The four claims are jointly inconsistent; the Catholic reply denies the fourth, the usual Orthodox reading denies the first.
premises: A pope teaching ex cathedra cannot teach heresy (Vatican I)
What an ecumenical council condemns as heresy is heretical
Constantinople III condemned Honorius's letter to Sergius as heresy
Honorius's letter was an ex cathedra definition
arguments.source: Constantinople III (681), 13th session, anathema of Honorius; Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus ch. 4 (1870); see Siecienski, The Papacy and the Orthodox (OUP 2017)

cruxes: Every ecumenical council is protected from doctrinal error
Florence was ecumenical
If the Filioque is false, Florence erred
The Filioque is false (as the Orthodox hold)
arguments.name: Council of Florence and the Filioque
arguments.note: Orthodoxy accepts the first claim and denies that Florence was ecumenical; Catholicism denies the fourth.
premises: Every ecumenical council is protected from doctrinal error
If the Filioque is false, Florence erred
The Filioque is false (as the Orthodox hold)
arguments.source: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439); Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381) without the Filioque; A. E. Siecienski, The Filioque (OUP 2010)
